rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: A hypocrite boasted he could divert the believers, praised Companions before them, then told his own companions to imitate him; the revelation exposed their intent.
rows.anchor: The occasion given for this revelation involves a hypocrite who boasted to his companions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites’ satans are variously understood as their leaders, fellow hypocrites, disbelievers, or inner demons.
rows.anchor: Here it is usually understood to mean the hypocrites’ leaders, fellow hypocrites, disbelievers, or inner demons

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quranic use of satans can include human beings as well as otherworldly beings, as 6:112 illustrates.
rows.anchor: At times in the Quran shayāṭīn refers not only to otherworldly creatures, but also to human beings

rows.speaker: Ṭ, R, Q
rows.claim: They read purchased as preferred, comparable to choosing blindness over guidance in 41:17.
rows.anchor: Here purchased can be understood as “preferred,” as in 41:17, they preferred blindness to guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commerce imagery makes the interpretation preferred less likely, despite its fit with an Arabic use of shirāʾ.
rows.anchor: though this reading is made less likely by the mention of commerce

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran elsewhere uses buying and selling as metaphors for spiritual matters.
rows.anchor: Such language relating buying and selling to spiritual matters is also found in 2:86; 2:175; 3:177

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: One reading takes the Covenant as humanity’s general duty to acknowledge God’s Oneness and worship Him, grounded in the pre-eternal covenant.
rows.anchor: the general obligation of human beings to acknowledge God’s Oneness and worship Him

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another reading identifies the Covenant with the Arabs’ oath to be more rightly guided if a warner came.
rows.anchor: it refers to And they swore by God their most solemn oaths

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation takes the Covenant as a specific one made with the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: or it refers to a specific covenant made with the People of the Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some understand what God commands to be joined as blood ties, whose reverence and maintenance are commanded elsewhere.
rows.anchor: Some say that what God has commanded be joined refers to blood ties

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Others understand the command to join broadly as any Divine Command to keep things joined.
rows.anchor: Others consider it to include any such Divine Command to keep things joined

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some note that Jews also had blood ties to the Prophet because Isaac and Ishmael were brothers.
rows.anchor: not only the Arabs had blood ties to the Prophet; the Jews did also

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāsir can describe being deprived of something or being lost by losing one’s way or self.
rows.anchor: khāsir can also denote “being lost” in the sense of losing one’s way or losing one’s self

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The theme of submission begun in 2:128 continues through Abraham, Jacob, and their children.
rows.anchor: from v. 128 continues through to Jacob and his children

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islām is Muhammad’s religion by proper name, but the Quran also uses it for primordial true religion and a universal orientation of the soul toward God bequeathed by prophets.
rows.anchor: generalized in the Quran to imply the primordial religion and true religion as such

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The Quran’s argument denies exclusive People of the Book ownership of the patriarchs, presenting them as followers of Abraham’s pure religion, primordial monotheism identified with Islam.
rows.anchor: the patriarchs named here cannot be claimed by the People of the Book in an exclusive and narrow way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s story is developed in Sūrah 12 through the account of his son Joseph, and Jacob appears in other prophet lists.
rows.anchor: The story of Jacob (Abraham’s grandson through Isaac) and his children is more fully discussed in Sūrah 12

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ilāh means the generic noun god, not the proper name Allāh.
rows.anchor: In this verse the God translates ilāh

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: One interpretation asks what drove them to deeds bringing them nearer the Fire; it is not patience that enables them to endure it.
rows.anchor: For some, this verse means, “What drove them to the deeds that brought them closer to the Fire?”

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Another interpretation asks what gives them patience toward the Fire so that they abandon truth for falsehood.
rows.anchor: or, “What gives them patience in relation to the Fire so that they abandon truth for falsehood?”

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: More generally, the phrase is a way of asking what made them do this.
rows.anchor: In a general sense it can be understood as a way of saying, “What made them do this?”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account assumes the familiar story in which the young David, chosen by Saul as Israel’s champion, kills Goliath with a sling stone.
rows.anchor: though a young boy, David is appointed by Saul to face Goliath as the Israelites’ champion

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: David’s wisdom means he inherited Samuel’s prophethood, while his sovereignty means he inherited Saul’s kingship.
rows.anchor: he inherited the prophethood of Samuel, and sovereignty, meaning he inherited the kingship of Saul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of David’s prophethood and reign is further described in 38:17–29.
rows.anchor: For further description of David and his prophethood and reign, see 38:17–29

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s repelling some people by means of others also prevents destruction of houses of worship in 22:40; here it averts corruption of the earth.
rows.anchor: Here it is the corruption of the earth as such that is averted through this repelling

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators agree that God uses good people to repel evil’s effects but offer different accounts of who repels whom.
rows.anchor: Commentators state that God uses good people to repel the effect of evil people, but offer different interpretations

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: One view says forty inward members of a spiritual hierarchy, the Substitutes, dispense divine grace and protection, each replaced when one dies.
rows.anchor: when one dies, that one is replaced by another person

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Another view says the prayerful and pious repel the impious, whose sins would otherwise destroy humanity.
rows.anchor: the prayerful and the pious are used to repel those who do not pray and are impious

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: A further interpretation is that the obedient repel the evil of the disobedient.
rows.anchor: the obedient repel the evil of the disobedient

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith says God repels punishment from people who do not pray, give alms, fast, make pilgrimage, or struggle through those who do.
rows.anchor: God repels the punishment of the one who does not pray by means of the one who prays

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the Quran’s longest single verse.
rows.anchor: This is the longest single verse in the Quran

rows.speaker: Ṭ, IK, Q
rows.claim: Although associated with agricultural forward sales, the rule generally applies to agreements including loans when payment and delivery are not simultaneous.
rows.anchor: It is said to have been revealed in connection with agricultural forward sales, but is generally applicable to all agreements, including loans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Madinah, forward sales allowed payment for agricultural goods due one to three years later; the Prophet required fixed quantity, weight, and delivery time.
rows.anchor: Whosoever contracts a forward sale, let it be for a set amount, a set weight, and a set time

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Forward sale is an exception to the ban on selling what one does not possess because agricultural sellers need funds for seeds and crop care on an annual cycle.
rows.anchor: This represents an exception to the general rule that one is prohibited from selling what one does not possess

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Though risky, forward sale is not gambling; its social benefit is considered greater than its possible harm and uncertainty.
rows.anchor: the social benefit is thought to outweigh the potential harm and uncertainty

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A seller must own production means and specify the product’s attributes, quantity, delivery time, and feasible place of delivery.
rows.anchor: the product should be of known traits and attributes

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The buyer should pay fungible or monetary material because agricultural sellers lack liquid wealth and hold assets not easily converted to money.
rows.anchor: they should pay in fungible or monetary material

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The debtor, broadly including a forward-sale seller, dictates the terms; commentators say the creditor may inflate the amount and the seller is usually weaker.
rows.anchor: The one who has to deliver the product or repay a loan, the debtor (used in the general sense

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Writing records the agreement’s terms for memory; it does not replace a living witness, since testimony was primarily oral and secondarily written.
rows.anchor: the writing was meant to serve as a means of remembering the terms of the agreement

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: A scribe’s duty to write contracts is communal: society must provide someone, but each individual need not do it.
rows.anchor: which means that someone in society must be available to carry out what is a solemn duty

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: The debtor described as feeble-minded, weak, or unable to dictate is interpreted respectively as mentally disabled, a minor, or incapacitated by illness.
rows.anchor: someone who is mentally disabled, a minor, or someone who is sick to the point of incapacitation

rows.speaker: IK, Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The one-man-and-two-women witness provision is specific to these commercial transactions and differs from other testimony.
rows.anchor: this provision is peculiar to the commercial transactions mentioned in this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses give equal consideration to male and female testimony in accusations of adultery by either spouse.
rows.anchor: where accusations of adultery are given equal consideration whether they are made by the husband or the wife

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Classical law generally excluded women’s testimony in corporal punishment and qiṣāṣ cases, though this appears to be preference because women could testify without a male witness.
rows.anchor: in the absence of a male witness, women’s testimony would be accepted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A judge cannot strictly quantify testimony’s value and needs all relevant evidence; the preferences likely reflect social aversion to involving women in these matters.
rows.anchor: a judge simply needs all the relevant evidence to come to a decision

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: To err means to forget an aspect of the contract.
rows.anchor: “to err” means to forget some aspect of the contract

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators differ over whether the reminded woman becomes legally equal to a man or the two women together equal one man; the latter view was more widely accepted.
rows.anchor: The latter was more widely accepted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators infer women’s essential inability to judge objectively and intrinsic unreliability as witnesses.
rows.anchor: some commentators, but not all, understood this verse to indicate an essential inferiority in women’s ability to judge objectively

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not demand an inference of female inferiority; its described transaction allows two women to arrange a sale and use two men as witnesses.
rows.anchor: Nothing in the verse demands such a reading, however

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Women may conduct sales and loans for themselves, including transactions without witnesses; the witness provision therefore serves another purpose.
rows.anchor: women, like men, can transact any sale or loan on their own behalf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because women of the time generally lacked experience with complex finance, two women could make testimony more practical and protect them from bullying or manipulation, rather than indicting their reliability.
rows.anchor: accepting two women in the place of one man would have been more practical

rows.speaker: Abū Bakr ibn ʿArabī
rows.claim: In Aḥkām al-Qur’ān he wondered why one man could not remind one woman if she erred, and found no answer.
rows.anchor: jurists such as Abū Bakr ibn ʿArabī, inAḥkām al-Qur’ān, wondered why

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The testimony stipulation is particular to this circumstance and addresses social or communal difficulties; the approval of witnesses also suggests competence in this specialized area.
rows.anchor: from among those whom you approve as witnesses suggests that it is a matter of competence in a specific area

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forward contracts could span years, and women might be less socially available to witness them over time; spot sales need no written contract because delivery and payment are simultaneous.
rows.anchor: The trade of present goods refers to a transaction where delivery is made at the time of payment

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Not finding a scribe can mean lacking the means to write the contract.
rows.anchor: And cannot find a scribe can also mean that one does not find the means with which to write the contract down

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A pledge is collateral given by a debtor to a creditor or by a forward-sale seller to a buyer as security without a written contract and witnesses.
rows.anchor: collateral property that is given by the debtor to the creditor, or the seller to the buyer in a forward sale

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse allows the parties to trust one another without taking property as a pledge.
rows.anchor: the verse then leaves open the possibility that one will trust the other party without taking a pledge

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some say the trust provision abrogates 2:282’s contract rules; many restrict it to travel and retain written contracts as the ordinary rule.
rows.anchor: many believe that this provision applies only in the special circumstance of the person being on a journey

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Be patient and vie in patience share the root ṣ-b-r; the second means outdo the enemy in patience and endurance.
rows.anchor: the second to a contest of patience in which one should outdo the enemy in patience and endurance (R, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rābiṭū comes from a root meaning tie, fortify, and join; ribāṭ generally conveys firmness and steadfastness, especially taking a frontier post for defense or anticipated attack.
rows.anchor: the word refers to taking up a border or frontier post (or to the post itself) in defense of the community

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The martial post is called ribāṭ because one ties or bridles one’s horse, as in the Quranic phrase for tethered horses.
rows.anchor: it is called ribāṭ because one “ties” or bridles one’s horse

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: Hadiths praise a day of ribāṭ above the world and all it contains, and say its merit can continue after death because community defense enables others’ piety.
rows.anchor: One day of ribāṭ in the way of God is better in God’s Eyes than this world and all that is in it

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet calls ablution in unpleasant conditions, many steps to the mosque, and waiting for one prayer after another ribāṭ.
rows.anchor: Performing ablutions under unpleasant conditions, multiplying one’s steps to the mosque, and waiting for the prayer after the prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waiting between canonical prayers means remaining in remembrance, devotion, and reflection; al-Nawawī compares this spiritual ribāṭ with martial ribāṭ.
rows.anchor: This is a spiritual ribāṭ, which is compared with the martial ribāṭ by the famous jurist al-Nawawī

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A well-known hadith says those returning from battle have come from lesser jihad to greater jihad, which the Prophet identifies as struggle against one’s passions.
rows.anchor: A servant’s jihād against his passions

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Sound judgment includes a working rational faculty, upright character, ability to manage property, and adequate religious soundness for independent custody.
rows.anchor: a correctly functioning rational faculty, a healthy and upstanding character, an understanding of how to manage property

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Many jurists set male maturity at eighteen; absent sound judgment then, some allow withholding property for at most seven more years.
rows.anchor: many to be eighteen for males according to Islamic Law

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Other views set maturity at fifteen or seventeen.
rows.anchor: Others put the age of maturity at fifteen or seventeen

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Another view uses the age of moral responsibility rather than a simple biological threshold such as puberty.
rows.anchor: it should be the age at which one is considered morally responsible rather than a simple biological threshold

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Judgment may be tested by giving orphans money and observing how they manage it.
rows.anchor: giving them some money and observing how they manage it

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Jurists disagree whether transfer requires both physical maturity and sound judgment or whether either alone is enough.
rows.anchor: whether the requirements for giving the orphans their property include both physical maturity and the development of sound judgment or if either alone suffices

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: A poor guardian may take only what necessities require, especially food; it is a loan that must be repaid even after death.
rows.anchor: they can take only as much as they need for necessities—particularly food—and it is considered a loan that must be repaid

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A guardian may use an orphan’s livestock milk, land’s fruit, or riding animals if value is maintained and no monetary profit is sought.
rows.anchor: The guardian may benefit from the milk of the orphan’s livestock, the fruit produced on the orphan’s land

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some say even the limited permission for a guardian to use orphan wealth was abrogated by 4:10.
rows.anchor: even this limited permission to consume orphans’ wealth was abrogated by v. 10

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Witnesses when delivering the orphan’s property are generally considered mandatory; some also require them when borrowing from the orphan’s property.
rows.anchor: The command to bring witnesses when giving orphans their property is generally considered mandatory

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran commonly calls those who disbelieve in life losers in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The Quran commonly refers to those who disbelieved in this life as being lost or “losers” in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who deny meeting God and suppose worldly life is all will suddenly recognize their error at the Hour, the Resurrection and universal judgment.
rows.anchor: thinking there is naught but our life in this world (v. 29), will have the realization of their error “come upon them suddenly”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their cry expresses regret that they failed to prepare for the coming day.
rows.anchor: Their cry, Alas for us, expresses their regret over failing to prepare for this day

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī explains their regret as existential anguish at wasting God-given intellect and faculties meant to disclose truth and cultivate virtue.
rows.anchor: a deep, existential regret, as disbelievers realize that they have squandered the intellect and other faculties bestowed upon them by God

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī compares their loss to an investment that earns no return and loses the borrowed principal as well.
rows.anchor: lose not only the anticipated return on an investment, but the borrowed principal as well

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The burdens on their backs may be their own sins and transgressions.
rows.anchor: may be their sins and transgressions themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the burden as God’s wrath earned by sin.
rows.anchor: or the burden of wrath from God that is earned as a result of those sins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further interpretation is the burden of warnings and reminders they ignored; 20:100–101 says the reminder becomes a Hereafter burden.
rows.anchor: or the burden of the warning and reminders they refused to heed in their earthly lives
